Average Variance Extracted (AVE)

Source: R/average_variance_extracted.R
average_variance_extracted.Rd

The average variance extracted (AVE) is the mean proportion of indicator variance a factor accounts for, a standard convergent validity summary for a reflective measurement block in confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling. With standardized loadings \(\ell_j\), $$\mathrm{AVE} = \frac{1}{J} \sum_j \ell_j^2.$$ The quantity itself is elementary. In a model with cross-loadings, an item contributes its loading to the AVE of every factor it loads on; the same shared variance then counts toward each factor's summary, so compare AVE values across factors of such a model with that overlap in mind. A loading the model holds at zero, fixed (0*item) or constrained (a*item with a == 0), is not a loading: the model written with it is the model written without it, and the item is not one of the factor's indicators. Fornell and Larcker (1981) are credited for establishing it as a validity criterion: a construct shows convergent validity when its AVE reaches the conventional 0.50 (the construct explains at least half its indicators' variance), and the Fornell-Larcker discriminant criterion compares each construct's AVE with its squared correlations with the other constructs. AVE is closely related to composite reliability (omega); for discriminant validity, htmt gives the heterotrait-monotrait ratio of correlations, a criterion that does not use the AVE.

Usage

average_variance_extracted(
  fit = NULL,
  loadings = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  ci_method = c("none", "percentile"),
  B = 1000L,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

fit

Optional lavaan fit of one group and one level (for example from cfa_1 or lavaan::cfa); the standardized loadings of every factor are extracted and one AVE is reported per factor. A fit whose optimizer did not converge, and a multiple-group or multilevel fit, are refused (see The fit under Details).

loadings

Optional numeric vector of standardized loadings for a single block, as an alternative to fit. Supply exactly one of fit and loadings. No interval can be constructed from loadings alone (their sampling variability is not carried by the numbers), so ci_method = "percentile" requires fit.

conf_level

Confidence level for the bootstrap interval (default 0.95); used when ci_method = "percentile".

ci_method

Interval method: "none" (the default) or "percentile". No closed-form interval for the AVE is in common use; the percentile bootstrap is the standard route in the validity literature. The cases in the fitted data are resampled with replacement B times, the model is refit to each resample, and each factor's interval is the pair of empirical quantiles of its B AVE values (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993). Replications whose refit fails or does not converge are set aside, and the interval is computed from those that return a value; a single warning reports how many were set aside, and gives the caution described under Details when it holds. A replication whose solution is improper for a factor is kept and counted (see Details). An interval requires that no more than half of the attempted replications were set aside and that at least the number the level requires returned an estimate (400 at the 95 percent level; see B). Otherwise the point estimates and counts are retained, with NA limits and a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient. These floors limit the error of drawing a finite number of resamples; they are not coverage guarantees.

B

Number of bootstrap replications when ci_method = "percentile", a single whole number. Default 1000, smaller than the package's usual 10000 because every replication refits the model; raise it for a reported analysis when time allows. The fewest accepted is 400 at the default conf_level (200 at 0.90, and 2000 at 0.99, which the default does not meet); a smaller or fractional B is refused before anything is computed (class dmar_count_invalid). See Details and dmar_bootstrap.

seed

Optional integer seed for the bootstrap. The default NULL uses the current state of the random number generator; a supplied seed is set internally and the prior state restored on exit.

Value

A data.frame (classes dmar_ave and dmar_tbl) with one row per factor: factor (label), ave, and ci_lower / ci_upper (the percentile bootstrap limits; NA when ci_method = "none"). All three are NA for a factor whose solution is improper (see Details). With ci_method = "percentile" and at least one factor whose solution is proper, so that an interval is formed, the table carries the attributes conf_level, B (requested), B_used (the replications the intervals rest on), n_dropped, B_required, and bootstrap_status (see Bootstrap replications under Details), and bootstrap, the counts in the form the reliability family records them (see reliability_omega): attempted (B), returned, failed (the replications whose refit failed or did not converge, which lavaan's bootstrap does not tell apart, counted in reasons as non-finite), reasons, error_messages, undetermined, improper, and no_solution (all zero here), improper_kept (the replications used whose solution was improper for at least one factor, including when its interval is withheld), not_converged (zero), refit_failed (the same count as failed, under the reason that the line under the table and the warning give for both causes, that the refit failed or did not converge), improper_rule ("keep"), caution, and improper_kept_by_factor, the improper replications kept for each factor, with factors_with_intervals recording which intervals were eligible.

Details

The fit. The AVE is read from a solution, so a fit whose optimizer did not converge (lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "converged") is FALSE, as when it reached its iteration limit) is refused with an error of class dmar_not_converged: its estimates mark where the optimizer stopped. A fit that converged to an improper solution is not refused; it is described under Improper solutions below.

A factor's standardized loadings are those of one group at one level. A factor of a multiple-group fit therefore has an AVE in each group, and a factor of a two-level fit has one at each level, even when it has the same name at both. Neither the unweighted mean of those values nor a mean weighted by group size is the AVE of any group, so the function describes a fit of one group and one level and refuses a multiple-group or multilevel fit with an error of class dmar_argument_invalid that names the groups (as groups) or the levels (as levels). The AVE of one group or level of such a model is average_variance_extracted(loadings = ) given the factor's standardized loadings in that group or at that level: the factor's column of that group's or level's lambda matrix in lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "std"), without the zeros of the items that do not load on it. For a group, a fit of the model to that group's data alone also gives it, without any equality constraints across groups.

Improper solutions. When the error variance of an indicator is estimated below zero (a Heywood case; for an ordered item, the residual variance of its latent response), its communality, one minus its standardized error variance, exceeds one, and so does its squared standardized loading in a model without cross-loadings. The AVE averages those communalities, so for a factor with such an indicator it is not a proportion of variance: its ave (and its interval) is NA, with a warning naming the indicators and their communalities, as in the measurement table of fa_confirmatory. On holzinger_swineford, a factor measured by visual perception and lozenges alone, beside one measured by general information, paragraph comprehension, and sentence completion, gives visual perception an error variance below zero and a communality of 1.30, so the first factor's AVE is NA (the mean of its squared standardized loadings would be .726), while the verbal factor's, .705, is reported. A larger sample, or reconsidering the model for those indicators, are the usual remedies.

No interval is formed for such a factor, so when every factor of the fit is improper the bootstrap is not run, and the table records no confidence level.

The bootstrap meets the same problem one resample at a time. A replication whose solution is improper for a factor that is proper in the observed fit is kept, as the reliability family keeps one under its default improper = "keep" (see reliability_omega), and counted. Its AVE for that factor averages a communality above one and can itself exceed one, so such replications gather in the upper tail of the factor's bootstrap distribution. The line printed under the table says how many replications were attempted, how many returned a value, and how many of those came from an improper solution, with, for two or more factors, the count for each; when the replications set aside and the improper ones kept for a factor reach the tail area beyond a limit, \((1 - C)/2\) of B for confidence level \(C\), it adds a caution, since the limits then depend on how those replications were treated; with two or more factors the caution gives the share of each factor it holds for, counted for that factor alone. The warning the call gives says the same, as the reliability family's does, naming each factor the caution holds for with its count. On 80 pupils drawn from holzinger_swineford (set.seed(113)), a factor of visual perception, cubes, and lozenges beside a verbal factor is proper in the sample, with an AVE of .449, but 101 of the 198 replications that returned a value were improper for it (B = 200, seed = 113), and its upper limit, 1.19, is not a proportion of variance; the verbal factor had none. With the 2 replications whose refit failed or did not converge, 103 of the 200 are in question for the spatial factor, against the 5 that lie beyond each limit of a .95 interval, and the warning names it. The counts are those the console and a knitted report print, and they are kept in the bootstrap attribute.

Bootstrap replications. The percentile interval reads its two limits from the quantiles of the B replicated AVE values of each factor, so it is run only when B puts at least 10 replications beyond each limit (400 at the 95 percent level). A replication in which an AVE is undefined (the refit failed or did not converge) is dropped and counted, never replaced, and the interval is computed from the rest. The result records B (requested), B_used (the number the interval rests on), n_dropped, and B_required (the fewest replications a request may ask for; that count is held to B, not to B_used) as attributes, beside the fuller bootstrap list, with bootstrap_status ("complete", "dropped", "exploratory", "insufficient_count", or "insufficient_share"). One warning of class dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped states the counts when any replication was dropped, with a caution when the dropped replications are at least the 2.5 percent of B that lies beyond one limit at the 95 percent level, because they could then decide by themselves where that limit falls. When more than half were dropped, the limits of every factor are NA, the estimate is returned, and the warning has class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient. options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) lets a smaller B (2 or more) run for a first look or a demonstration; every such call gives a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_exploratory and the result is not one to report. See dmar_bootstrap for the rule and its reasons.

The percentile bootstrap interval resamples the cases behind fit and refits the model once per replication, so its cost is B model fits. That refitting is why the examples below stop at the point estimates: the fewest replications a 95 percent interval is reported from, B = 400, run well beyond the time an example is given on the two-factor model there. To obtain the interval, pass ci_method = "percentile" together with a seed, as in average_variance_extracted(fit, ci_method = "percentile", seed = 113), and keep the default B = 1000 or more for a reported analysis.

A supplied two-stage fit requires eligible unrestricted first-stage moments. Bootstrap intervals currently refuse separately stored two-stage auxiliary variables because the refits do not carry their resampled values. Resample and refit items and auxiliaries together explicitly when that analysis is needed.

References

Efron, B., & Tibshirani, R. J. (1993). An introduction to the bootstrap. New York, NY: Chapman & Hall/CRC.

Fornell, C., & Larcker, D. F. (1981). Evaluating structural equation models with unobservable variables and measurement error. Journal of Marketing Research, 18(1), 39–50.

See also

htmt for discriminant validity; reliability_omega for the composite reliability of the same block (coefficient omega is what the composite-reliability literature computes); cfa_1 to obtain the fit.

Other multivariate and latent variable methods: bifactor_indices(), cfa_1(), cfa_2(), ci_bifactor_indices(), ci_eigenvalue(), common_method_adjusted_r(), common_method_marker(), common_method_single_factor(), compare_sem(), dmacs(), ecvi(), equivalence_rmsea(), fa_bifactor(), fa_confirmatory(), fa_second_order(), factor_congruence(), factor_scores(), htmt(), irt_grm(), irt_information(), measurement_alignment(), measurement_invariance(), procrustes_phi(), sem_exact_fit_bootstrap(), sem_fit_measures(), sem_information_criteria(), sem_residual_fit(), simple_structure()

Examples

# Directly from the standardized loadings a paper reports:
average_variance_extracted(loadings = c(.8, .7, .6))
#>  factor ave   ci_lower ci_upper
#>  f      0.497 <NA>     <NA>    

# From a fitted model, one AVE per factor (requires lavaan).
data(holzinger_swineford)
fit <- lavaan::cfa(
  "verbal    =~ t6_paragraph_comprehension + t7_sentence +
                t9_word_meaning
   deduction =~ t20_deduction + t22_problem_reasoning +
                t23_series_completion",
  data = holzinger_swineford)
ave_tbl <- average_variance_extracted(fit)
ave_tbl
#>  factor    ave   ci_lower ci_upper
#>  deduction 0.469 <NA>     <NA>    
#>  verbal    0.719 <NA>     <NA>    

# The Fornell and Larcker (1981) discriminant criterion compares each
# factor's AVE with the squared correlation between the factors: a
# factor should account for more of its own indicators' variance than
# it shares with the other factor. Here the comparison favors verbal
# and goes against deduction, whose AVE falls below the shared
# variance. Fitting with fa_confirmatory(..., output = "measurement") puts the
# AVE values and the latent correlations in one table.
lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "cor.lv")["verbal", "deduction"]^2
#> [1] 0.5327517

# The broom verbs: one row per factor.
generics::tidy(ave_tbl)
#>        term  estimate estimand ci_lower ci_upper conf_level
#> 1 deduction 0.4694312      ave       NA       NA         NA
#> 2    verbal 0.7193173      ave       NA       NA         NA
generics::glance(ave_tbl)
#>   n_terms conf_level B_used
#> 1       2         NA     NA
